Guilliman is a fictional primarch described as a genetically engineered war-leader in Warhammer 40,000.
After the fictional Horus Heresy, Guilliman’s Codex Astartes sets out the division of Space Marine Legions into Chapters.
Within the fiction, dividing Space Marine forces is intended to prevent any single force from threatening the Imperium again.
The chapter compares Diocletian’s distribution of imperial responsibility with Guilliman’s division of military power.
Both responses can be interpreted as efforts to manage danger through structural changes.
Diocletian governed a historical state, while Guilliman’s code belongs to a fictional setting centered on interstellar war and superhuman soldiers.
Warhammer 40,000 is modern fiction and should not be treated as a direct account of Roman history.
The eastern Roman Empire, commonly called the Byzantine Empire, continued for roughly a millennium after the western empire’s fall.
The Byzantine state preserved Roman political identity while adapting institutions and military practices to changing pressures.
The chapter contrasts Diocletian’s governmental restructuring with Guilliman’s fictional code for restraining Space Marine forces.

claims_detail.text: The Templars and Hospitallers joined religious life with armed service in the Crusader world.
Comparing the orders with Space Marines does not prove direct historical inspiration.
In the early twelfth century, Latin Christian travelers journeyed to holy places amid political contest and danger.
Around 1119, knights associated with Hugh of Payns organized to protect pilgrims near Jerusalem.
The Knights Templar became a religious military order combining communal discipline and fighting service.
The Templars received formal recognition at the Council of Troyes in 1129.
The Hospitallers joined religious vocation with warfare in their history.
The Hospitaller order grew from a Jerusalem hospital and later developed a military role in the Latin East.
The Templars are chiefly remembered as a fighting order, while the Hospitallers also emphasized care for the sick and poor.
Both orders were institutions shaped by vows, rules, patrons, and changing political circumstances.
Medieval military orders adapted religious discipline to lives that could include combat.
Members of military orders were not monks in every technical sense, and ranks and obligations varied.
The warrior-monk image combines obedience, communal rule, austerity, devotion, and the material realities of warfare.
A vow in this context publicly committed a person to a community and way of life.
Adeptus Astartes are fictional genetically transformed superhuman soldiers serving the Imperium in Warhammer 40,000.
Space Marine chapters are depicted with hierarchy, ritual, inherited traditions, and religious-order imagery.
Space Marine imagery can evoke sacred vestments, monastic rules, and battle as service to a higher cause.
Space Marines are not simply Templars in power armor.
The comparison rests on the shared image of discipline and violence under devoted service.
The historical orders and the fictional Astartes differ profoundly.
The Templars and Hospitallers were historical human communities embedded in medieval institutions and conflicts.
Space Marines are fictional transhuman warriors in a far-future universe.
Medieval religious vows and military-order rules are not equivalent to fictional Astartes transformation and doctrine.
Placing the orders beside the Astartes traces a motif rather than a documented chain of descent.
Religious discipline joined to armed service creates a narrative pattern of devoted, rule-bound warriors.
The comparison highlights what different worlds sanctify and what they ask warriors to surrender.
Crusader-world vows bound people to religious institutions amid political struggles and human costs.
Space Marines turn the image of religiously disciplined warriors into far-future mythic imagery.
A resemblance is not proof of direct influence.
The next chapter can explore the institutions and legends that sustained the warrior-monk ideal.
